questions.solution: The most notorious derivative of morphine is heroin. It is synthesized by acetylation of the two hydroxyl groups of morphine with acetyl chloride, hence its other names, diacetylmorphine or diamorphine. Once heroin enters the brain, it is converted to morphine and binds rapidly to opioid receptors. Abusers typically report feeling a surge of pleasurable sensation—a “rush.” The intensity of the rush is a function of how much drug is taken and how rapidly the drug enters the brain and binds to the opioid receptors. With heroin, the rush is usually accompanied by a warm flushing of the skin, dry mouth, and a heavy feeling in the extremities, which may be accompanied by nausea, vomiting, and severe itching. After the initial effects, users usually will be drowsy for several hours; mental function is clouded; heart function slows, and breathing is also severely slowed, sometimes enough to be life-threatening. Slowed breathing can also lead to coma and permanent brain damage

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.q: Erythroblastosis foetalis can be seen in marriage between
questions.solution: A special case of Rh incompatibility (mismatching) has been observed between the Rh-ve blood of a pregnant mother with Rh+ve blood of the foetus. Rh antigens of the foetus do not get exposed to the Rh-ve blood of the mother in the first pregnancy as the two types of blood are well separated by the placenta. However, during the delivery of the first child, there is a possibility of exposure of the maternal blood to small amounts of the Rh+ve blood from the foetus. In such cases, the mother starts preparing antibodies against Rh antigen in her blood. In case of her subsequent pregnancies, the Rh antibodies from the mother (Rh-ve) can leak into the blood of the foetus (Rh+ve) and destroy the foetal RBCs. This could be fatal to the foetus or could cause severe anaemia and jaundice to the baby. This condition is called erythroblastosis foetalis. This can be avoided by administering anti-Rh antibodies to the mother immediately after the delivery of the first child. Since the only antibody which can pass through the placenta is IgG, anti-Rh antibodies are actually a type IgG antibody.

questions.solution: Attacking the macrophage HIV reservoir has proven a thornier issue. From the virus's standpoint, macrophages are an ideal reservoir cell because they are long-lived, because HIV does not kill macrophages by direct lysis, as it does CD4+T cells, and because virus production by chronically infected macrophages tends to be relatively insensitive to a variety of antiretroviral agents. Besides hosting a significant virus reservoir, chronically infected macrophages and/or their brain counterparts, microglia, may contribute to pathogenesis through the chronic aberrant release of a variety of host and viral cytoactive factors and may be subject to chronic dysregulation through the aberrant expression of surface receptors.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.q: The type of immunity that is present at the time of birth in humans is:
questions.solution:
The innate immune system, also known as non-specific immune system, is the first line of defence. It comprises the cells and mechanisms that defend the host from infection by other organisms in a non-specific manner. This means that the cells of the innate system recognize and respond to pathogens in a generic way. Innate Immunity is present at the time of birth. Innate immunity consists of four types of barriers.

• Physical barriers: Skin on our body is the main barrier which prevents entry of the micro-organisms. Mucus coating of the epithelium lining the respiratory, gastrointestinal and urogenital tracts also help in trapping microbes entering our body.

• Physiological barriers: Acid in stomach, saliva in the mouth, tears from eyes all prevent microbial growth.

• Cellular barriers: Certain types of leukocytes (WBC) of our body such as polymorph nuclear leukocytes (PMNL-neutrophils) and monocytes and natural killer cells in the blood as well as macrophages in tissues can phagocytise and destroy microbes.

• Cytokine barriers: Virus-infected cells secrete proteins called interferon which protect non-infected cells from further viral infection.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.q: The correct order of stages in life cycle of Plasmodium is
questions.solution: Mosquitoes ingest the Plasmodium while feeding on an infected human. The malarial parasite is in the haploid Gametocyte stage. There are two types of plasmodial gametocytes: Microgametocytes and Macrogametocytes. Once ingested, One Microgametocyte undergoes a process of exflagellation to form 8 flagellated haploid male gametes (microgametes). One Macrogametocyte undergoes differentiation to form one haploid female gamete (macrogamete). This takes place within the mosquito's gut (crop). These male flagellated male gametes fertilize the female gamete to form a diploid zygote within the mosquito's gut (crop). This diploid zygote develops a motile stage is called ookinete. This ookinete penetrates the gut lining and develops a protective covering around it within the gut wall. This is called the oocyst stage. The cell within the oocyst undergo repeated divisions to form thousands of sporozoites.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.q: Which of the following stages of Plasmodium is correctly depicted in the transmission between female Anopheles mosquito and humans?
questions.solution: When the female Anopheles mosquitoes bite humans for a blood meal, they inject the sporozoites of Plasmodium into the skin wound. Thus sporozoite stage is the infective stage of Plasmodium in humans. These sporozoites reach the blood stream and migrate to liver. They infect liver cells (hepatocytes) where they divide asexually to form many merozoites. These merozoites rupture the liver cells and escape into bloodstream. Each merozoite infects an erythrocyte where it develops into ring form followed by trophozoite which shows intracellular feeding followed by schizont which in turn produce many merozoites. These newly formed merozoites come out of the erythrocytes by rupturing them. The rupture of erythrocytes causes release of a toxic substance, haemozoin, which is responsible for the chill and high fever. Some of these merozoites escape the asexual amplification cycle and form microgametocytes and microgametocytes. Their further development requires cooler temperature found in mosquitoes. These gametocytes are stored in erythrocytes till they are transferred to female Anopheles mosquito.

MRI uses strong magnetic fields and non-ionising radiations to accurately detect pathological and physiological changes in the living tissue. Antibodies against cancer-specific antigens are also used for detection of certain cancers. Tumor cells have been shown to avoid detection and destruction by immune system. Therefore, the patients are given substances called biological response modifiers such as alpha-interferon which activates their immune system and helps in destroying the tumor.

transformation of the cells by reducing the dependence of cells on growth like factors and thus undergo uncontrolled cell division.

Cancer cells grow very rapidly, invading, and damaging the surrounding normal tissues. As these cells actively divide and grow they also starve the normal cells by competing for vital nutrients. They secrete chemicals that promote the formation of new blood vessels for the cancer cells. This is called angiogenesis. Cells sloughed from such tumors reach distant sites through blood, and wherever they get lodged in the body, they start a new tumor there. This process is called metastasis

questions.solution: Hallucinations mean perception of an image or sound in the absence of its actual stimuli. The effects seen are alterations in mood, perception, thoughts etc. Many such products are obtained from Cannabis. Hence these drugs are also known as psychodelic drugs. questions.subject: Zoology
questions.q: Other than sexual contact, HIV is transmitted through
questions.solution: Transmission of HIV-infection generally occurs by (a) sexual contact with infected person, (b) by transfusion of contaminated blood and blood products, (c) by sharing infected needles as in the case of intravenous drug abusers and (d) from infected mother to her child through placenta. So, people who are at high risk of getting this infection includes - individuals who have multiple sexual partners, drug addicts who take drugs intravenously, individuals who require repeated blood transfusions and children born to an HIV infected mother. It is important to note that HIV/AIDS is not spread by mere touch or physical contact; it spreads only through body fluids. It is, hence, imperative, for the physical and psychological well-being, that the HIV/AIDS infected persons are not isolated from family and society.

questions.solution:
Autoimmune diseases are certain unrelated disorders caused by inflammation and destruction of tissues by the body's own immune responce. These disorders include acquired haemolytic anaemia, pernicious anaemia, rheumatic fever, rheumatoid arthritis, glomerulonephritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, myasthenia gravis, Sjogren's syndrome, and several forms of thyroid dysfunction, including Hashimoto's disease.

Angiogenesis: It refers to the formation of new blood vessels, which ultimately helps in providing the nutrient to the tumors to show metastasis.

Metastasis: This refers to the ability of tumor cell to spread or move from one site to other distant sites through the blood and initiate the formation of tumor and angiogenesis.

questions.q: Antibody molecule is Y shaped. The two tips of this Y shaped molecule bind to antigen through which type of interaction/bond?
questions.solution: The typical structure of immunoglobulin or antibody is Y shaped and is represented as <math><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></math>. This means it consists of two heavy chains and two light chains. These chains are polypeptide chains and because of difference in weights one is termed as heavy and other is termed as light. Both these chains are linked by disulphide bonds. Each chain consists of two regions: constant region or FC i.e. fragment crystallizable and variable region or Fab i.e. fragment for antigen-binding region. Thus the variable region consists of antigen-binding site that is a part of heavy and light chains. Antigens are attached to antibodies through non-covalent bonds.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.q: Where will you look for the gametes of a malarial parasite?
options: Red blood corpuscles of humans suffering from malaria
Salivary glands of freshly moulted infected female mosquito
Gut of infected female mosquito that can act as vector for malaria parasite
questions.solution:
Malaria is cause by the parasite Plasmodium and it is spread by the female mosquito which feeds off the blood from animals for nutrients. Thus, the female mosquito acts as the vector for transmitting the disease.

During a blood meal by the mosquito, blood stage parasites (gametocytes, which occur in male and female forms) are ingested and pass in to the gut of the vector mosquito. These gametes mate in the gut of the mosquito and begin a cycle of growth and multiplication in the mosquito. Thus, gametes of the parasite will be found the gut of the mosquito.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.q: Select the disease which is NOT an auto-immune disorder.
questions.solution: A condition where the body's own immune system mistakenly attacks the body cells/tissues is called as autoimmune disorder.  Mysathenia gravis (neuromuscular disorder where the skeletal muscles are weakened), Grave's disease (hyperthyroidism, overactive thyroid), Rheumatoid arthritis (inflamed joints) are type autoimmune diseases. Muscular dystrophy is genetic disorder which damages and weakens the muscles overtime due to lack of the protein dystropin. This protein is necessary form normal function of the muscle.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.q: Phagocytosis may be characterized by which of the following statements?
options: It involves fluid uptake by small vesicles
It is important in digestive processes in mammals
It involves the uptake of cellular debris in large endocytic vesicles.
questions.solution:
The immune cells like macrophages have the ability to "eat" or "devour" pathogenic cells by ingesting them. This process of cell-eating is called phagocytosis. Phagocytosis can be defined as a process to ingest of engulf other cells or particles. The ingested particle is surrounded by a vesicle called endocytic vesicles that help in digestion.

Phagocytosis is a type of endocytosis. If a cell takes is fluid substances making endocytic vesicle is called pinocytosis.

questions.subject: Zoology

questions.solution: Infection caused by Entamoeba histolytica, of Entamoeba group is called amoebiasis. It is also called amoebic dysentery. Symptoms may include ulcerations, diarrhea or bloody diarrhea.

common cold affects upper respiratory tract while in pneumonia lower respiratory tract including lungs is infected

there is no vaccine available to prevent either of the two diseases

The common cold affects the upper respiratory tract while pneumonia affects the lower respiratory tract. Both are infectious conditions.

questions.subject: Zoology

questions.solution: The primary lymphoid organ such as bone marrow and thymus provide the micro-environments for the development and maturation of T-lymphocytes. Here the immature lymphocytes differentiate into antigen-sensitive lymphocytes.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.q: Haemozoin is a toxic substance released upon which of the following events?
options: Rupture of cells of gut epithelium
Rupture of cells of salivary glands
questions.solution: The Plasmodium species during malarial formation, metabolize hemoglobin and other RBC proteins to create a toxic pigment called hemozoin. Haemozoin is a waste product formed when the parasite digests the blood. The parasite digests the hemoglobin of the blood and release high quantities of free heme. This heme released is a non-protein component of hemoglobin. The haemozoin is, therefore, a product of the erythrocyte lysis released from the food vacuole into circulation.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.q: Which of the following is a secondary lymphoid organ?
questions.solution: Lymphoid organs can be primary or secondary. Primary organs are those that form and mature lymphocytes from progenitor cells. These are Bone marrow and thymus. Secondary organs are those where interaction takes place between the lymphocytes and thus immune responses are generated. These include lymph nodes, Peyer's patches, MALT (Mucosal associated lymphoid tissue) etc.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.q: Active immunity means
questions.solution: Active immunity is formed after exposure to an antigen. It can occur when any microbe or antigen enters a person's body who has yet not come in contact with the same earlier. Thus the body did not have any antibodies earlier. This immunity helps to create antibodies for this first time exposure too but this is a very slow process. Thus active immunity is resistance developed through the formation of antibodies.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.q: Which of the following events are NOT associated with the phase/cycle of malarial parasite in man?
questions.solution: Plasmodium causes malaria. It requires two hosts: man and mosquito to complete its cycle. Sporozoites are infectious agents of malarial parasites. When a female mosquito bites the human, these enter the bloodstream. Inside the body these have an erythrocytic and exoerythrocytic cycle. When in the human body, the infectious agent undergoes many developmental stages (asexual reproduction). It also produces a toxin known as hemozoin inside the body and this is responsible for various symptoms like fever, chills, etc. When healthy mosquito bites such an infected human, these agents enter the mosquito's body and start its sexual reproduction which transforms into various forms and reside in the salivary gland. This healthy mosquito is now an infected one and if this again bites any human, the same cycle continues. Thus the pathogen cannot form a zygote in man because the sexual reproduction is completed in the mosquito's body.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.q: The principle of immunization or vaccination is based on which property of the immune system?
questions.solution: There are two types of immunity. innate and Acquired. Innate immunity is the immunity that is present since birth. It is very different from Acquired immunity as it is nonspecific. Acquired immunity is also known as Adaptive immunity. It is very specific and thus can differentiate between self and non self. Another main difference between Innate and Acquired is that Acquired immunity not only protects the body from infections but also prepares the body for further attack. This is due to the formation of memory cells. Acquired immunity is again of two types: AMI (Antibody mediated immunity) and CMI (Cell mediated immunity). Immunity can also be classified as Active and Passive. Active immunity is the introduction of Antigens which induces formation of Antibodies and this can be done Naturally or Artificially. Artificially it is done by use of Vaccines. Vaccines are live or attenuated pathogens which trigger the memory cells and also formation of Antibodies. But the main principle is to retain memory.

questions.solution: Salmonella typhi is a pathogenic bacterium which causes typhoid fever in human beings. These pathogens generally enter the small intestine through food and water contaminated with them and migrate to other organs through blood. Sustained high fever (39° to 40°C), weakness, stomach pain, constipation, headache and loss of appetite are some of the common symptoms of this disease. Intestinal perforation and death may occur in severe cases. Typhoid fever could be confirmed by Widal test. A classic case in medicine, that of Mary Mallon nicknamed Typhoid Mary, is worth mentioning here. She was a cook by profession and was a typhoid carrier who continued to spread typhoid for several years through the food she prepared.

questions.solution: Anamnestic response is a highly intensified and strong response and is characterized by a high titre of antibodies. It is also known as the secondary immune response. But, when the immune system comes in contact with the antigen subsequently, the immune response is highly intensified and massive, as the immune system was previously sensitized with this antigen. This is the anamnestic response.

(i) Secretion of interferons is a cytokine barrier of innate immunity. Interferons are proteins secreted by the virus-infected cells, which prevent the non-infected cells, from getting the infection.

(ii) T-lymphocytes are responsible for providing cell-mediated immunity. They do it through the synthesis of substances like cytokines.

(iii) Injection given against snake venom is a type of passive immunization. It contains preformed antibodies against the snake venom in it.

(iv) Antibodies which are produced during allergic reactions are of IgE type.

questions.solution:
The mucus coating of epithelium lining of the respiratory, gastrointestinal and urogenital tract belong to the physical barrier of innate immunity. They trap the microbes which enter our body and thus prevent infection.

Cytokine barrier includes proteins called interferon, which are secreted by virus infected cells and provide protection to non-infected cells.

Cellular barrier includes the leucocytes present in the body and macrophages, which are phagocytic in nature.

questions.solution:
The condition which develops after entering this new place is known as allergy or hypersensitivity. There might be certain substances like pollen, dust, etc. present in this place to which the immune system is allergic or hypersensitive to. The immune system thus responds to this antigen in a highly exaggerated manner. The symptoms include watery eyes, runny nose, sneezing, itching, etc. The antibodies which are produced in this response are of the IgE type.

The chemicals which are released in an allergic response include histamine and serotonin which are released by the mast cells. Adrenaline has no role to play in an allergic reaction. It is a hormone produced by the adrenal medulla in situations of emergency and result into increased heart rate, etc. vasodilation, etc.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.q: Which of the following is an incorrect statement about the second response of the body against a previously infected antigen?
options: The main antibody formed during the secondary response against a previously encountered antigen is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>IgM.</mi></math>
The secondary immune response of the body is based on memory cells.
The immune response against a previously infected antigen is also known as anamnestic response.
The secondary immune response gives effective immunity.
questions.solution:
Acquired immunity is pathogen-specific. It is characterised by memory. This means when our body encounters a pathogen for the first time it produces a response called primary response which is of low intensity. Subsequent encounter with the same pathogen elicits a highly intensified secondary or anamnestic response. This is ascribed to the fact that our body appears to have memory of the first encounter. The  primary and secondary immune responses are carried out with the help of two special types of lymphocytes present in our blood, i.e., B-lymphocytes and T-lymphocytes.

The B-lymphocytes produce an army of proteins in response to pathogens into our blood to fight with them. These proteins are called antibodies. The T-cells themselves do not secrete antibodies but help B-cells to produce them. Different types of antibodies are produced in our body. IgA, IgM, IgE and IgG are some of them. Though IgG is the most common antibody formed by the memory cells, IgA- and IgE-expressing B-cells play an important role in the secondary immune response.

questions.solution: The principle of immunization or vaccination is based on the property of ‘memory’ of the immune system. In vaccination, a preparation of antigenic proteins of pathogen or inactivated/weakened pathogen (vaccine) is introduced into the body. The antibodies are produced in the body against these antigens, and they neutralize the pathogenic agents during actual infection. The vaccines also generate memory – B and T-cells that recognize the pathogen quickly on subsequent exposure and overwhelm the invaders with a massive production of antibodies.

Transformation of normal cells into cancerous neoplastic cells may be induced by physical, chemical or biological agents. These agents are called carcinogens. Ionising radiations like X-rays and gamma rays and non-ionizing radiations like UV cause DNA damage leading to neoplastic transformation. The chemical carcinogens present in tobacco smoke have been identified as a major cause of lung cancer. Cancer causing viruses called oncogenic viruses have genes called viral oncogenes.
